title: 🎙️ Science, Wonder & the Natural World
description: Today we look at scientific discovery and the natural world — from ecology and wildlife research to astronomy and deep-sea biology. We're grounding these stories in the landscapes and living systems of the Cariboo: what salmon runs, boreal forest research, or species-at-risk studies tell us about the wild places we live beside. We're after stories that inspire curiosity and wonder about how the world works. - Daily themed article selection for podcast generation

_podcast.theme_description: Today we look at scientific discovery and the natural world — from ecology and wildlife research to astronomy and deep-sea biology. We're grounding these stories in the landscapes and living systems of the Cariboo: what salmon runs, boreal forest research, or species-at-risk studies tell us about the wild places we live beside. We're after stories that inspire curiosity and wonder about how the world works.
_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt: Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Science, Wonder & the Natural World' — scientific discovery, ecology, natural phenomena, and the curiosity-driven study of living systems. Strong fits include: wildlife biology and species research, ecology studies and biodiversity findings, watershed and salmon research relevant to BC, astronomy and space science, new species discoveries, citizen science projects, natural history stories, wildfire science and forest ecology, climate science findings (not just policy), geology, evolution, and deep-time Earth stories, and any scientific research grounded in BC or Cariboo landscapes and ecosystems. Prefer articles that convey genuine curiosity and discovery — the 'how' and 'why' of the natural world. Score 70–90 for: prehistoric life and palaeontology (ancient oceans, Cretaceous ecology, deep-time species), new species discoveries in ocean or remote environments, deep-sea biology, evolutionary biology findings, natural history stories with a strong sense of wonder, and field research grounded in BC ecosystems. Penalise (score 0–30): consumer health and pharmaceutical research without ecology or natural-world context; pure policy and advocacy news; technology business stories without a science or ecology angle; human interest and viral news without scientific substance; geopolitical and crime news. Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [Fast Company] Measles outbreaks surge to top 3,500 cases this year: These tracker maps show the areas hardest hit
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The United States has reached an ignominious milestone this week.

According to data from the International Vaccine Access Center at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, measles cases have now surpassed the 3,500 mark—a level not seen in 35 years.

Here’s what you need to know about the multiple outbreaks affecting the country, and which areas are currently being hit the hardest.

What’s happened?

According to the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, as of September 18, 3,568 measles cases were reported in the United States this year so far.

More worryingly, nearly 10% of those cases—341 of them—occurred in the previous two weeks leading up to September 18.

The figure is nearly 1,300 more than the total U.S. measles cases reported in all of 2025, and a level not seen since 1991, when the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says measles cases reached 9,643.

Speaking of those CDC numbers, if you look at the agency’s official data up to September 18, you’ll see it differs slightly from the John Hopkins’s data. According to the CDC, measles cases for 2026 in the U.S. stand at 3,471 as of September 18. That’s a discrepancy of 97.

The difference seems to stem from the timeframes and the data the CDC uses to update its official measles dashboard, including, as the Guardian noted, how it registers measles deaths.

The CDC says its dashboard is updated with “only confirmed measles cases notified to CDC as of noon on Thursdays,” while John Hopkins updates its dashboard on Fridays “with intermittent updates as warranted.”

Why is measles surging in the United States?

Regardless of which current tally you go by, there’s no disputing that measles is running rampant in America compared to the historic number of cases going back the last three decades.

Measles was officially declared eradicated in America in 2000, with only dozens to a few hundred cases popping up in most years between 2000 and 2018. But then in 2019, measles cases spiked to more than 1,200, according to CDC data. 

Cases dropped again during the pandemic as social distancing made the spread of the virus harder, but then in 2025 they surged to nearly 2,300, and in 2026, cases now top 3,500.

And it’s not just America. As reported by UNICEF USA last November, measles cases are rising globally.

But why? UNICEF says there are two main culprits: rising vaccine hesitancy and public health funding cuts. Both have accelerated in the U.S. since 2025, when measles cases began skyrocketing in the country.

Mapping measles in the U.S.

Both the CDC and John Hopkins have maps that track the number of measles cases across the country.

The CDC’s most recent map shows that in 2026, measles cases have been reported in all but five states.

The five states with no reported cases are Arkansas, Hawaii, Mississippi, Nevada, and New Hampshire.

But those are the outliers. The map shows that nine states have reported more than 100 cases each, with the top three states reporting more than 500 cases each.

The worst state when it comes to the number of cases is Pennsylvania, where an outbreak is ongoing. That state so far has had 745 cases in 2026. South Carolina comes in second with 670 cases this year, and Utah third with 527 cases.

John Hopkins’s measles tracker map corroborates those state rankings on a year-to-date basis. However, the university also offers another map that covers just the last two-week period, which helps to visualize where outbreaks are currently occurring.

According to that map, for the September 4 to September 18 period, 314 cases have been confirmed, with the majority—193 of them—happening in Pennsylvania. Ohio is the next state with the highest number of cases, at 58. Wisconsin follows in third place with 20 cases.

items.title: [Fast Company] OpenAI is accused of taking dangerous cyber risks for ‘private gain’ in lawsuit over rogue AI agents
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

In what is now one of many known cases, OpenAI’s agents went rogue in July, launching a cyberattack on Hugging Face.

Now, the ChatGPT maker is being sued over that incident and the other attacks that have since come to light—such as its not-so-casual hacking of an Australian national healthcare database. 

Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology (LASST), a self-described public interest nonprofit, has sued OpenAI in San Francisco’s Superior Court. 

LASST alleges that OpenAI violated California’s Comprehensive Data Access and Fraud Act (CDAFA) by accessing computer systems without the other party’s authorization.

The suit notes that California doesn’t allow for the defense to argue that “artificial intelligence autonomously caused the harm to the plaintiff.” 

As Tyler Whitmer, founder and CEO of LASST, put it in a statement: “AI companies are building agents that act autonomously making decisions, taking actions, accessing systems, without human direction at every step. California law is very clear: companies cannot escape responsibility for what their agents do.”

Fast Company has reached out to OpenAI for comment.

“Gravity of the harm”

LASST is also alleging that OpenAI is in violation of the Unfair Competition Law’s unfairness prong.

The “conduct is independently unfair because the gravity of the harm it causes vastly outweighs any utility or justification for it, and because the conduct is immoral, unethical, oppressive, and substantially injurious,” the group bluntly states. 

The suit further points to OpenAI’s response to the attacks as an “unfair business practice.”

In late August, the AI startup, which recently delayed what is expected to be one of the largest IPOs in history, issued an open letter that called for every AI company to “make cyber defense an immediate leadership priority.”

It warned that “In the coming months, AI-enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable.”

LASST alleges this is unfair positioning as OpenAI is responsible for such cyber risks and is taking dangerous measures for “private gain.” 

OpenAI has launched a site dedicated to “misalignments reports and notices,” along with creating a timeline of these dangerous incidents and its responses. The company claims to be working on additional safeguards, among other protections. 

The nonprofit isn’t seeking any monetary damages in the suit—though OpenAI might prefer giving up money to the actual goal: regulation.

LASST has asked for a court order “prohibiting OpenAI’s AI agents from accessing third-party computer systems without permission, and forbidding OpenAI from continuing to employ unsafe AI development practices that threaten serious harm to the public.”

items.title: [Fast Company] Most workers are working on Sundays—here’s why
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Nearly three-quarters of workers (74%) work on Sunday, including 21% who work a full or near-full day, according to Owl Labs’ tenth annual State of Hybrid Work report.

The trend is far more common among younger generations, with 76% of Gen Z workers and 62% of millennials saying they often work on Sunday, compared to 34% of baby boomers and 42% of Gen Xers.

The report says AI adoption may partly explain the spread of Sunday work. Nearly two-thirds (62%) of respondents said AI has increased what they’re expected to accomplish in a day, and 46% say it sometimes hinders their productivity.

Another potential culprit is meeting fatigue: 38% of workers said meetings leave them overburdened during the week, citing overly long meetings (45%), too many meetings overall (41%), and too many back-to-back meetings (34%).

Workers are also adopting a more flexible approach to scheduling in general. Nearly two-thirds (61%) expressed interest in “microshifting,” or working in “short, non-linear blocks to manage [their] workday around parenting, health, energy levels, or [their] personal productivity.”

Owl Labs, a Boston-based provider of videoconferencing solutions, surveyed 2,000 full-time knowledge workers in the U.S. on issues related to remote, hybrid, and in-office work.

Overall, the percentage of workers in the office full-time rose from 63% to 65% in 2025, and the percentage on a hybrid schedule fell from 28% to 25%. However, flexible work remains broadly popular: 46% of respondents said they would work a hybrid schedule if they could.

The report also reflects the newfound ubiquity of AI, with 82% of employees saying they use it, including 90% of Gen Z. The share who said they use it daily climbed from 27% to 32% year over year.

The rise of AI has had both benefits and drawbacks. On the positive side, 69% of workers said AI has made them more productive and 66% said it has boosted their confidence. However, 46% said it sometimes hinders their productivity, and another 46% worry AI could make their roles unnecessary.

AI use was more common among managers (92%) than individual contributors (62%).
